heard: NASA never spent millions developing a space pen. Early U.S. and Soviet missions relied on standard pencils. However, broken pencil graphite tips and wood shavings posed electrical shorts and eye hazards in zero gravity. Pencils also presented a severe fire hazard in spacecraft oxygen environments. Paul C. Fisher spent around $1 million of his own private capital to develop the pen. Fisher patented the AG-7 anti-gravity pen in 1965 using pressurized nitrogen gas. NASA ordered 400 pens in 1968, and the Soviet Union later bought 100 for Soyuz missions. Both space agencies ended up adopting the exact same pen because NASA never spent millions developing a space pen. in.
